Knifemare is correct on PSU's, down to the brands to buy. SeaSonic is the gold (platinum+ ?) standard, but you're going to pay gold for that standard. These are better options for your dollar.

I see you're buying an overclockable CPU with an overclockable motherboard. You're intending to purchase an aftermarket cooling solution for your overclocking habit, right? And if you're not planning on overclocking your overpurchasing when you get a K processor or Z board.

Very good then. Carry on. Just switch out the PSU.

The manufacturer of your motherboard will have a list of compatible memory. I recommend grabbing something off their list. Should be in the Mobo user manual which you should be able to get from the manufacturers website.

K CPU's and Z- mobo's are not necessary for entry level stuff. The 'K' and the 'Z' are pretty much a label for overclocking enthusiasts, meaning that CPU can be overclocked and the Mobo has some extra doo-dads that make overclocking easier in one way or another. If you're not looking to run a stable overclock you could save a bit by dropping the 'K' CPU and 'Z' board denominations.

If you plan on using Chrome you'll need another 128Gb of RAM.

Make sure your PSU has the appropriate cables for your GPU. No point getting to build day and realising you need an 8 pin power for GPU and only have 6 pins on your PSU.

Buy an earthing clip thingy, goes around your wrist and attaches to shit to discharge static. I've never had shit go wrong but you never know.

Don't pull your components out of the crinkly (anti-static) bags then place them on top! The inside of the bag is designed to prevent static, the outside is not and could be holding a charge that will damage components.

No matter what anyone ever tells you, no computer part is hard to put in. Most things will only go in one way. Check, check again, then insert. At most you'll need a firm, even pressure to insert a component. RAM is probably the most stand-out in terms of force required to seat. You CPU does not need to be forced down, it should sit gently in its place and be held down by the bracket on the socket.

Enjoy PC gaming.

That is a complicated question.Computer components generally have specific requirements as to what other computer components they will work with..For example CPUs fit into a socket on your motherboard and that differs depending on which cpu you are buying and from which company.Ram comes in different speeds and different types,Video cards have different power requirements and may require extra power connectors etc.There is no definitive guide to what components to pick as this varies depending on cost and and what other components you have.My best advice is to take some time and read up different computer components and and what is involved in building a pc.There are plenty of resources on the net.If you have specific questions then come back here and ask.I am sure everybody will be willing to help.

Does anyone have any online resources where you can learn about these compatibility issues? I was raised with computers, but I'm definitely no IT or hardware guy. Last time I built a computer was 10 years ago.

I used PCPartPicker.com when I did my build in November. Everything worked fine with no conflicts. PCPartPicker will give you what "should" work together. I usually read the Newegg reviews to see if the parts are lemons. Tomshardware and a few other sites usually have good reviews on what different devices in a certain class will do in comparison to each other (I.E. Z87 vs. H87 motherboards).

I've built a few PCs over my decades and it's really hard to be incompatible as long as your CPU fits your board. As far as upgradable, in my experience, pick the processor you want/can afford then look at the board. Three times I picked my mobo first thinking I would just upgrade the processor later. Never..ever..happened. RAM is easy to add/replace later so don't sweat that. GPUs have gotten so insanely better that I can't even keep up with them anymore, just find the best you can afford for your socket. The main problem I've had with video cards is making sure it has clearance in your case.

This is a link that has helped with my last two builds and is updated regularly. http://www.logicalincrements.com/

If you can wait I would hold for Skylake, the processor itself is nothing special other than a die shrink but the motherboard will pack a ton of new features. Its going to be a huge jump from the current motherboard space.

Bad: Sugar, carbs. Good: Lean, protein, fiber. This advice sounds simple but somehow manages to confuse me.

 

I'm fairly certain I was either never educated about food in grade school, or I didn't pay attention. When I went off to college I had no money so I ate what was cheap: pasta. I was very physically active and never snacked. I was probably burning the pasta carbs as fast as I could eat them.

When I finished college and got a desk job, pasta remained my go-to meal but now with the addition of ice cream for dessert because I finally had both time to snack and money for sweet things. I also was very sedentary because I sat at a desk all day instead of being physically active. Within just a few months, my entire body composition changed. This was almost ten years ago. I've since joined and quit 2 gyms, changed my diet a number of times with no success. I'm always hungry, which leads me to believe I'm not choosing appropriate foods when I eat.

 

I no longer eat any pasta nor any ice cream. I also walk at least the 10 000 steps per day recommended by the American Heart Association. (I was previously at 2 000 to 3 000 steps per day!)

I often skip breakfast because I don't make time for it, or I just drink a glass of 1% fat chocolate milk or a glass of V8 vegetable juice (not tomato juice). If someone ordered pizza the night before, I'll have 2 slices cold the next morning. On rare days I make 2 or 3 packets of Walmart brand instant oatmeal (I always try for 2, but if it comes out too runny I add the 3rd packet to make it thicker.)

Lunch typically looks like this: Diced frozen chicken, mixed frozen veggies (always peas, usually green beans, carrots, broccoli, sometimes cauliflower), alfredo sauce, garlic powder. I have no idea how many ounces anything is. Throw it all in a 6" x 6" x 2" square plastic container, put it in my backpack, and microwave it for 2 minutes when it's lunch time. Or Taco Bell if it's a nice day and I can walk there from work. I drink about 2-3 litres of water throughout the day.

Dinner typically looks like this: Frozen fish fillet (usually breaded, sometimes not), tartar sauce, more of the same mixed frozen veggies used to make my lunch, then some fries, tots, or onion rings with ketchup or chipotle sauce. Sometimes I do black beans and instant brown rice instead of fish. I have no idea about ounces or anything for dinner either. If a roommate orders pizza or goes for tacos I'll get in on that instead of making something myself. My evening beverage is usually more chocolate milk or fruit juice, sometimes with various forms of alcohol mixed with the juice if it's been one of those days.

If I snack between meals, it's typically gluten free chips with Tostitos brand spinach dip, or Totinos pizza rolls (10 of them, probably enough calories to make an entire meal of better food).

On the days I eat pizza and tacos, I'm sure those aren't healthy choices. On the days I have vegetable juice, chicken with veggies, fish with veggies, I think I've made the best choices, but I still feel hungry in between meals and I'm sure I could make some little changes which would go a long way.

 

I think I've provided as much information here as I can. Let me know if something's missing. I am going to try to do less of the tacos, pizza, and juice/alcohol. Would someone please suggest further changes, maybe some way to help me feel fuller on fewer calories? Thanks in advance!

EDIT: 25 days later and I'm down 5 lbs. Now that I've got more of a routine with counting what I eat, I hope the next 5 lbs will be faster. I'm not in any rush, though, and I realize there's more I need to change to be healthy than just a number on a scale. Thanks for all the advice so far!

Have you ever calculated your basal metabolic rate? If not, do this for me, and for yourself:

  1. Read about and calculate your BMR (lots of online calculators)

  2. Eat 500 calories less than that everyday for 2 weeks, just 14 days. To do this you MUST count calories.

  3. Weight train for 20 minutes a day 3 days each week, and keep walking.

  4. For every glass of soda or coffee you have, drink 2 glasses of water. Be sure to stay hydrated.
